# B2 — is any denial path unattributed? (findings, pass 1)

**Instrument:** code-only, laptop, `HEAD = 1fe34c8`. Every message below was **generated by
running the real binary**, not read off the source: the broker was rebuilt
(`cargo build`, to avoid the stale-binary trap) and driven through 34 sbatch-side refusals,
19 step-side refusals and 9 egress-proxy refusals with hand-written spool requests and a
live `--net-proxy`. Harnesses:
`scratchpad/drive.sh`, `drive-step.sh`, `drive-proxy.sh` (session scratchpad, not in the repo).

## Summary

husk has **73 distinct refusal messages** across 11 files, and the enumeration is not a null
result. The *policy* refusals — the ones husk wrote on purpose, with a rationale comment above
them — are uniformly excellent: attributed, actionable, and **byte-identical on retry
(verified mechanically: two independent broker runs, `diff` clean on all 34 sbatch messages,
all 19 step messages, and the entire generated guard script)**. The failures are all in the
seams: **13 refusals carry no husk attribution at all**, and because both stubs prefix their
output with `sbatch: error:` / `srun: error:`, those 13 do not merely *lack* attribution — they
arrive **wearing SLURM's own name**, which is worse than the 22 anonymous `EROFS` lines this
brief exists for. Three messages assert a cause husk cannot know or knows to be wrong, one of
which (`F1`) tells the agent to ask its operator for a change that is *guaranteed to be refused*
and that would silently disable the whole job's egress if the operator complied. And the
writable-set banner — husk's single most load-bearing pre-announcement — **makes a false claim
("reads are unrestricted") and understates its own read-only carve-outs inside the announced
writable root**, which is a pre-announcement that actively misleads rather than one that is
merely missing. The kernel-enforced side is half-covered: read-only root is well announced,
`SIGSYS` is translated at job level but not at step level, and **`--unshare-net` with no
allowlist configured is announced nowhere at all**.

---

## THE TABLE

**Legend.** `✓` pass · `✗` fail · `△` partial/qualified · `—` not applicable.
`P5 = —` means the rule costs nothing beyond "remove the option and resubmit", so there is no
consequence to bear; it is not a free pass.
**Delivery** column: `stub` = reaches the agent through `sbatch-stub.py:35` /
`srun-stub.py:37`, i.e. prefixed `<tool>: error:` — *this prefix is why an unattributed body is
actively mis-attributed to SLURM.* `job` = echoed to the job's stderr by the generated guard.
`http` = written into the caged client's HTTP stream. `log` = broker/session log only.

## Findings, most severe first

### F1 — the 403 tells the agent to ask for a change that CANNOT be granted, and that breaks all egress if it is · CONFIRMED

`netproxy.rs:196`–`203` produces one message for two very different denials:

> `husk: example.com:6817 is not on husk's network allowlist. Ask your operator to add it to sandbox.network.allowedDomains if the work genuinely needs it.`

Reproduced live (`drive-proxy.sh`, allowlist = `example.com`): `example.com` **is** on the
allowlist. The refusal is `netallow.rs:256` — `SCHEDULER_PORTS = [6817,6818,6819,6820]` is an
unconditional block checked *before* the entries, because reaching slurmctld from a cage is
AV8, the broker-bypass this project exists to prevent.

Three failures at once:

* **P6 (correctly scoped):** it states a cause husk knows is false. The port was not "missing
  from the list"; it is permanently barred.
* **P1 (actionable):** the remedy is impossible. `Entry::parse` (`netallow.rs:155`–`158`)
  rejects any entry naming a scheduler port.
* **Worse than useless:** an operator who follows the advice makes `Allowlist::parse` return
  `Err`, so `net_proxy_mode` (`main.rs:305`–`311`) exits 1 and **the job loses all egress**,
  with the explanation only in the job log. The one denial that most needs to be understood is
  the one most confidently misdescribed — and the fix it recommends silently disables the
  feature.

The same message also fires for a malformed request host (`netallow.rs:253`,
`is_valid_request_host`), which is again a different cause. Note the *operator-facing*
message for the identical rule (`netallow.rs:72`–`77`) is exemplary — it names AV8 and
explains. The agent-facing one throws all of that away.

### F2 — a `--chdir` that merely does not exist is reported as a confinement violation · CONFIRMED

`policy.rs:307`–`316` → `settings::confine_under_any` (`settings.rs:204`–`222`). The helper
tries every writable root, **discards the real error** (`Some(_) =>` at `settings.rs:214`
ignores the bound value) and always emits the set-membership message. Reproduced (case `c18`,
`--chdir=<project>/nope`, where `<project>` *is* the only writable root):

> `--chdir: "…/proj/nope" is not inside any directory this job may write. husk confines --chdir/--output/--error to the writable set … Writable here: …/proj`

The path is plainly inside the directory the message names as writable. The real cause is that
`canonicalize` failed with ENOENT. An agent reading this will conclude its confinement model is
wrong and start moving directories around; the fix is `mkdir`. Note the asymmetry that proves
it is a bug and not a choice: the **same underlying condition** on `--output` (case `c24`) is
diagnosed correctly — "cannot be resolved … It must already exist" — because
`confine_output_pattern` calls `confine_under_workdir` directly and keeps its error.

### F3 — the "output directory must exist" refusal is husk's rule but is attributed to SLURM · CONFIRMED

`settings.rs:227`–`231`, reached for `--output`/`--error`:

> `--output: "…/proj/nodir" cannot be resolved (No such file or directory (os error 2)). It must already exist — SLURM does not create output directories.`

Delivered as `sbatch: error: --output: …`. No "husk" anywhere, and the one named party is
**SLURM**. But real `sbatch` accepts a non-existent output directory at submit time; it is husk
that refuses here, because it canonicalises the path to confine it. So the message hands the
agent a false model of who is refusing and why — the exact "confident, wrong remediation"
shape B2 exists to prevent. (`settings.rs:226`, "cannot resolve the working directory", has the
same attribution gap but is unreachable in practice, since `--chdir` was already canonicalised.)

### F4 — three refusals are byte-for-byte indistinguishable from real sbatch/srun errors · CONFIRMED

`sbatch.rs:353`, `:368`, `:370`, reached from **both** registries. Captured verbatim:

```
sbatch: error: option '--exclusive' does not take a value
sbatch: error: option '--time' requires a value
sbatch: error: value "$(rm -rf ~)" for '--job-name' is not allowed (must match the option's safe grammar)
srun:   error: option '--label' does not take a value
srun:   error: value "abc" for '--ntasks' is not allowed (must match the option's safe grammar)
```

The stub prefix (`sbatch-stub.py:35`, `srun-stub.py:37`) mimics the real tool, so the *only*
signal that husk is involved is the message body — and here there is none. This is a
mis-attribution, not merely a missing attribution: the agent is told SLURM refused, so it will
never look for husk's rule, and "safe grammar" names a concept that exists nowhere in SLURM's
documentation while never saying whose it is or what it permits. Same defect, lower blast
radius, in rows 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, 29, 39, 48, 49, 51, 52, 54 — 13 unattributed refusals in total.

### F5 — a failure caused by husk's own forced options is reported as SLURM's · PLAUSIBLE

`spool.rs:408`–`412` returns `sbatch failed: <the real sbatch's stderr>`, delivered as
`sbatch: error: sbatch failed: …`. The command line husk submitted is **not** the one the agent
wrote: husk forces `--partition`, `--account`, `--nodes=1`, `--export=ALL`, `--chdir`,
`--output`, `--error`. So a site rejection of a husk-forced value (`Invalid account or
account/partition combination`, an unavailable forced partition, a `cli_filter` rule) surfaces
as an unexplained SLURM error about a submission the agent cannot see, with nothing naming the
forced values or pointing at the session log. Not reproducible without a cluster, hence
PLAUSIBLE; the code path is unambiguous. The remedy that fits husk's own doctrine is one line
naming the forced options, exactly as the `--account` refusal (row 12) already does.

### F6 — the `#SBATCH <Forced>` refusal names the wrong reason for four of its nine triggers · CONFIRMED

`sbatch.rs:452`. Reproduced for `#SBATCH --wrap=x`:

> `#SBATCH --wrap is controlled by the broker and can't be set by the job (output/error/chdir/export are forced to safe values). Remove it.`

The parenthetical enumerates four options; the message fires for any `Class::Forced` option not
handled elsewhere, and `--wrap` is not among them (nor is the reason "forced to a safe value" —
`--wrap` is refused outright). Minor P1/P6: the agent is given an explanation that does not
describe its own case, and "the broker" never says *whose* broker.

### F7 — the partition refusal asserts a property of partitions husk cannot know · PLAUSIBLE

`policy.rs:450`–`455`, on every partition refusal: *"These are typically preemptible/low-priority,
so checkpoint your work."* The allowed set is operator configuration
(`HUSK_SLURM_PARTITION`); reproduced with `short, pp-short`, the message still asserts it,
and on Balfrin those are not preemptible partitions. This is exactly the P3 failure that
produced the original "spoofed message" episode, one level milder: an agent that checks
`sinfo` finds husk saying something observably off about a partition it named itself. Hedged by
"typically", hence PLAUSIBLE rather than confirmed. Everything else in this message is the best
in the codebase.

### F8 — a seccomp kill is translated for the job but not for a step · PLAUSIBLE

`policy.rs:975`–`981` turns exit status 159 into a message naming `seccomp-wrapper` and telling
the reader how to identify the blocked call. The step path has no equivalent: `step.rs:169`–`175`
reports `step exited with status {code}`, and `srun` propagates a signal-killed task as
128+31 = 159. So an MPI rank killed by the filter produces `srun: error: step exited with
status 159` — no husk, no seccomp, no remedy — while the identical event at job level produces
five attributed lines. The asymmetry inside husk's own code is CONFIRMED; the exact numeral
needs hardware, hence the verdict. This matters more than it looks: ranks are where new
syscalls actually appear (the CUDA/`cuInit -> 304` and CMA/`EPERM` episodes were both this
shape), and "read the errno before widening a filter" needs the errno to survive.

### F9 — one refusal string is unreachable · CONFIRMED

`sbatch.rs:323` ("unexpected argument … in the option list") cannot fire from either entry
point: `split_options_and_rest_in` (`sbatch.rs:226`–`251`) stops at the first token that is not
an option or a consumed value, so `interpret_cli_in` never sees a bare token in option
position. Verified by probe (`c30`, argv `["-","x"]`, accepted). Dead code in a default-deny
gate is worth knowing about — it is a rule nobody can test — but it is not a hole.

### F10 — the cage banner makes a false claim and understates its own carve-outs · CONFIRMED

`policy.rs:538`–`556`, the single most load-bearing announcement husk emits, and the direct
answer to the 22-`EROFS` field report. Generated verbatim:

```
husk: compute cage active - the filesystem is READ-ONLY except:
husk:   /…/proj  (project dir: where husk was launched)
husk: reads are unrestricted. A write outside the list above fails
husk: with 'Read-only file system' - that is husk, not the filesystem.
```

Against the bwrap arguments generated **from the same call** (`settings.rs::bwrap_args`,
dumped from the guard):

1. **"reads are unrestricted" is false.** `--tmpfs /users` hides every home; each `denyRead`
   directory becomes a `--tmpfs`; each credential file becomes `--ro-bind /dev/null <path>`.
   These denials produce **no errno at all** — an empty directory, an empty file — so they are
   the one denial class an agent cannot detect by trying, and the banner has just told it not
   to suspect husk. That is worse than the anonymous `EROFS`: silence plus a disclaimer.
2. **The announced writable root is not fully writable.** Inside `<root>`, the cage emits
   `--ro-bind-try <root>/.git/config` and `<root>/.mcp.json` → `EROFS` **inside** the directory
   the banner names as the exception, and the banner's own next sentence ("a write outside the
   list above fails") tells the agent that cannot happen.
3. **Four paths inside the writable root accept writes that vanish.** `--tmpfs <root>/.claude`,
   `<root>/.git/hooks`, `<root>/.vscode`, `<root>/.idea` (the F6b auto-exec masks). A job
   writing `.claude/settings.json` sees success, no error, and no effect. Silent, and in the
   direction the agent least expects.

The mechanism is correct in every case; only the announcement is wrong. The fix is a banner
derived from the same list the cage is built from rather than from `writable` alone — which is
this project's own recurring lesson (one fact, one construction).

### F11 — three rank refusals interpolate a pid or a job id, breaking byte-identity · CONFIRMED

`rank.rs:262` and `:268` embed `/proc/<holder_pid>/ns/{user,pid}`; `rank.rs:275` embeds
`/dev/shm/husk-<SLURM_JOB_ID>`. The brief names pids and ids explicitly as property-4 breakers:
a retry produces a different string, so the message reads as a transient fault rather than
standing policy — the opposite of what made the partition guard work. The diagnostic value of
the path is real; a stable sentence plus the variable path on a second line would keep both.
Low severity (these are rare, fatal, and operator-facing in practice).

### F12 — two proxy refusals are delivered as a silent connection reset · CONFIRMED

`netproxy.rs:181`–`184` returns `Verdict::Refused` **without writing anything to the client**
for all three `read_head` failures: head > 8 KiB (`:124`), client closed (`:129`), and the 15 s
`READ_TIMEOUT` (`:131`). Reproduced: an oversize head yields `ConnectionResetError` with no
body. The module's own doc comment (`netproxy.rs:52`) states the requirement this violates —
*"A refusal says what was refused and why, on the job's own connection: a silent drop would be
indistinguishable from a network fault and would cost somebody an afternoon."* The size and
timeout caps are policy (they are DoS controls), so they deserve the 400 the other parse
failures get. The refusal *is* logged on the trusted side, which is where it matters for audit —
this is a teaching gap, not a containment one.

### F13 — four config-time denials emit nothing at all · CONFIRMED

`settings.rs:552` (`drop_symlinked_carveouts`), `:559` (`drop_floor_overlapping_allows`) and
`:670`/`:673` (relative `allowRead` skipped for the compute cage) discard operator
configuration silently. The operator's `allowRead` is in force on login and absent on compute,
or absent everywhere, with nothing said in the session log. The limiting case of an
unattributed denial is one with no output whatsoever. Note that the neighbouring
credential-scan truncation (`settings.rs:535`) does warn, and its comment states the principle
— *"Never fail silently"* — so this is an inconsistency within one file rather than a
disagreement about policy. Collides with B3/B5; handed over rather than resolved here.

### F14 — "this job has no network" is announced only when the network *feature* is configured · CONFIRMED

When no `sandbox.network.allowedDomains` exists, `policy.rs:643` takes the `else` branch:
`net_start` and `net_relay` are empty. The cage still gets `--unshare-net` (`settings.rs:813`),
so the job has no route at all — and the generated guard contains **no announcement of that
fact**. Verified by grep on the generated script: all 12 occurrences of "network" are shell
comments; every `echo` about the network lives in the enabled branch. So the default deployment
is the one with no pre-announcement, while all five failure modes of the *enabled* path are
carefully announced. An agent whose `pip install` fails gets a bare DNS error and no reason to
suspect husk — the F10 pattern in a second dimension. One unconditional banner line ("this job
has no network / this job may reach: …") would close it, and it is the same line either way.

### F15 — the login-side cage has no writable-set announcement at all · PLAUSIBLE

`grep -rn "READ-ONLY except\|HUSK_WRITABLE"` finds the banner only in `policy.rs::cage_banner`
and its two golden files — i.e. **inside a compute job**. The agent spends most of its life on
the login node, inside a bwrap cage built from the same `FsPolicy`, where an `EROFS` or a
masked home produces exactly the anonymous failure the compute banner was written to fix. The
denial messages there come from the vendored runtime and from the harness's permission layer,
neither of which names husk. Marked PLAUSIBLE because the login cage is partly out of husk's
code today (ROADMAP 6a), and because the argument is by symmetry rather than by reproducer —
but the symmetry is exact, and the fix (print the same banner at session start) is cheaper than
the one already shipped.

## What I checked that was fine

* **Property 4 (stable) is verified mechanically, not asserted.** Two independent broker runs
  in two different directories: all 34 sbatch-side messages, all 19 step-side messages and the
  **entire generated guard script** diff clean after normalising the deliberately-different
  test root. No message interpolates a timestamp, a random id or an unordered collection. The
  three genuine variances are F11 (pid/job id), row 30 (`Submitted this session:` grows as the
  session submits — correct behaviour, and `BTreeSet` keeps the order deterministic) and row 79
  (the resolver's own error text).
* **The policy refusals with a rationale comment above them are the best work in the file.**
  Rows 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 22, 27, 28, 30, 40, 41 score clean on every applicable property; row 69
  (terminated early) is the reference implementation of P6 — it states the fact and the
  consequence and explicitly refuses to name preemption vs wall limit vs scancel; row 5 carries
  the inherited wall limit as a consequence *and* concedes that other partitions may be idle,
  which is the P3 fix earned from the spoofed-message episode.
* **The wall-limit note is attached on the accepted path too**, not only on refusal
  (`policy.rs:374`), and suppressed correctly when the job set its own `--time` and when the
  allowed set has more than one partition. Verified live with a stubbed `scontrol`.
* **Both stubs pass the broker's message through unedited** (`sbatch-stub.py:215`,
  `srun-stub.py:155`) — no truncation, no reformatting, no swallowing. `where_to_look()`
  (`sbatch-stub.py:39`) points at the session log on every stub-side failure.
* **The `Class::Rejected` design is right.** `sbatch.rs:29`–`33` explains why a dropped option
  and a refused option must be different things; nine of the ten srun reasons are specific and
  useful, and six of them name husk.
* **The 403's placement is right.** The gate is one call on the name the client asked for
  (`netproxy.rs:196`), the dial uses the same name, and the refusal is logged on the trusted
  side (`netproxy.rs:279`) so the record of what a job reached does not depend on the job.
* **Operator-facing config refusals are attributed and actionable throughout** (netallow's
  seven `EntryError`s, `check_socket_path`'s six, the wrapper's fail-closed launch path) — with
  the four silent exceptions in F13.

## Collisions handed to A7 (not resolved here)

* Row 30 (`spool.rs:232`) discloses **this session's job ids** in the refusal body.
* Row 5 / the banner disclose the **allowed partitions** and the **exact writable roots**.
* The F14 fix would disclose the **egress allowlist** to the job. F10's fix would disclose the
  **credential mask list** — that one probably must stay a *count*, not a list, and A7 should
  say which.
